title: Percentage Calculator
introEs: Find what X% of a number is, instantly.
explanationEs: A percentage expresses a quantity as a portion of one hundred, which is why the word literally means 'per hundred.' When you find a percentage of a number, you are scaling that number down or up to the share the percentage represents. The percentage calculator does this in two clean steps: it converts the stated percentage into its decimal equivalent by dividing by 100, then multiplies that decimal by the value you are measuring against. Working 20% of 150, for instance, turns 20 into 0.2 and returns 0.2 times 150, which is 30. Percentages matter because they let people compare quantities on a common scale regardless of the underlying totals, so a 20% share means the same relative amount whether the base is 150 or 15,000. This shared scale is what makes the decimal-and-multiply method the standard approach; it mirrors the definition of a percentage exactly and avoids the rounding drift that mental shortcuts introduce. The tool removes that friction entirely and keeps the result exact. Shoppers use a percentage calculator for discounts and sales tax, students apply it to test scores and lab results, and finance and retail professionals lean on it for margins, tips, commissions and interest. Anywhere a part-of-a-whole relationship appears, this percentage calculator turns it into a precise figure.

faqs.question: What is a percentage?
faqs.answer: A percentage is a way of writing a number as a fraction of one hundred, marked by the percent sign. Saying 20% is identical to saying 20 out of 100, or the decimal 0.2. Because every percentage shares the same base of one hundred, percentages let you compare portions drawn from totals of any size on one consistent scale, which is what makes them so widely used.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a percentage of a number?
faqs.answer: Turn the percentage into a decimal by dividing it by 100, then multiply that decimal by the number you are measuring. For 20% of 150, divide 20 by 100 to get 0.2, then multiply by 150 to reach 30. The order never changes the answer, and doing both steps keeps the figure exact rather than rounded from a mental estimate.

faqs.question: How do I convert a percentage to a decimal?
faqs.answer: Divide the percentage by 100, which shifts the decimal point two places to the left. That converts 20% into 0.2 and 5% into 0.05. Reversing the process by multiplying a decimal by 100 turns it back into a percentage, so 0.2 becomes 20%. This conversion is the first step in almost every percentage calculation and keeps the arithmetic aligned with the definition of a percent.

faqs.question: Can I use this to work out a discount?
faqs.answer: Yes. Find the percentage of the original price first, then subtract it. On a 150 item marked 20% off, take 20% of 150, which is 30, and subtract to reach a sale price of 120. To go the other way and add sales tax or a tip, calculate the percentage the same way and add it to the base amount instead of subtracting.

faqs.question: Why divide by 100 instead of using the percentage number directly?
faqs.answer: The percent sign already means divided by one hundred, so 20% is not the number 20; it is 20/100, or 0.2. Multiplying a value by the raw 20 would scale it twenty times over instead of taking a fifth of it. Dividing by 100 first restores the intended proportion, which is why 20% of 150 correctly gives 30 rather than 3,000.

title: Percentage Increase Calculator
introEs: Calculate the percent change between two values.
explanationEs: Percent change captures how much a value has grown or shrunk compared with where it started, expressed as a proportion of that original amount. Because it is relative rather than absolute, a rise of 50 means very different things against a base of 200 than against a base of 5,000, and the percentage tells you which. The percentage increase calculator measures this by subtracting the original value from the new value, dividing that gap by the original, and multiplying by 100. Moving from 200 to 250 produces a 50 difference over a base of 200, which is a 25% increase; a negative result signals a decrease instead. Anchoring the change to the starting value is what makes the method meaningful, because growth is almost always judged against the point it grew from. That framing is why the same tool doubles as a percentage decrease calculator: the arithmetic is identical and only the sign flips. A percentage increase calculator keeps the direction and the magnitude in one figure. Analysts use it for revenue and price growth, scientists for measured change between readings, and everyday users for pay rises, rent hikes and portfolio swings. Whenever a before-and-after pair needs a single comparable number, this percentage increase calculator supplies it cleanly.

faqs.question: What is percent change?
faqs.answer: Percent change is the size of an increase or decrease written as a percentage of the original value. It answers how much something grew or fell relative to its starting point rather than in raw units. Reporting a move from 200 to 250 as a 25% increase is more informative than saying it rose by 50, because the percentage already accounts for the base the change is measured against.

faqs.question: How do I calculate percentage increase?
faqs.answer: Subtract the original value from the new value, divide the result by the original, then multiply by 100. Going from 200 to 250 gives a difference of 50; dividing 50 by 200 gives 0.25, and multiplying by 100 gives a 25% increase. The same three steps handle a decrease automatically, since a smaller new value makes the difference negative and the percentage falls below zero.

faqs.question: What does a negative result mean?
faqs.answer: A negative percentage means the value dropped rather than rose, so the calculator is reporting a decrease. The magnitude still works the same way, measured against the original amount. Because the formula subtracts the original from the new value, any new value lower than the original produces a negative numerator and therefore a negative percent, which is the signal that the quantity shrank.

faqs.question: Is percentage increase the same as percentage difference?
faqs.answer: No. Percentage increase is measured against the original value and carries a direction, so reversing the two numbers changes the answer. Percentage difference divides by the average of the two values and ignores direction, giving the same result whichever way you enter them. Use percentage increase when one number is clearly a starting point and the other an outcome; use percentage difference when neither comes first.

faqs.question: Can I use it to calculate a percentage decrease?
faqs.answer: Yes. The formula is identical for decreases: enter the original value first and the smaller new value second, and the result comes out negative to show the drop. Falling from 250 back to 200 gives a difference of minus 50 over a base of 250, which is a 20% decrease. Note that a rise and the matching fall are not equal percentages, because each is measured against a different starting value.

title: Percentage Difference Calculator
introEs: Compare two values as a percentage difference.
explanationEs: Percentage difference measures how far apart two values are relative to their typical size, without labelling either one as the reference point. Instead of asking how much A grew into B, it treats the two numbers even-handedly: it takes the absolute gap between them and compares it against their average. That symmetry is the defining trait, so the percentage difference calculator returns the same answer whether you enter 40 then 60 or 60 then 40, because swapping them changes neither the gap nor the average. The method matters when there is no natural before or after. Comparing two lab measurements, two suppliers' prices or two sensor readings, you rarely want one to count as the baseline; dividing by the average rather than by either value keeps the comparison neutral. For 40 and 60 the gap is 20, the average is 50, and 20 over 50 is a 40% difference. A percentage difference calculator applies that consistently and always reports a non-negative figure. Engineers, scientists, accountants and quality analysts reach for this percentage difference calculator when they need an unbiased comparison of two equal-standing quantities rather than a directional change from a fixed origin.

faqs.question: What is percentage difference?
faqs.answer: Percentage difference is the gap between two values expressed as a percentage of their average. It compares two numbers that stand on equal footing, with neither treated as the original or the reference. Because it divides by the average of the pair, it is symmetric: the values 40 and 60 differ by 40% no matter which you list first, and the answer is always zero or positive.

faqs.question: How is percentage difference different from percentage change?
faqs.answer: Percentage change divides by the original value and has a direction, so it tells you how much one number grew or shrank into another. Percentage difference divides by the average of the two values and has no direction, so it simply measures how far apart they are. Change suits before-and-after comparisons; difference suits two readings where neither is the starting point.

faqs.question: When should I use percentage difference?
faqs.answer: Use it whenever the two values you are comparing have no natural order: two independent measurements, two competing quotes, two instruments reading the same thing. In those cases picking one as the baseline would bias the result, so dividing by the average keeps the comparison fair. If one number is clearly a before and the other an after, percentage change is the better fit instead.

faqs.question: Can percentage difference be negative?
faqs.answer: No. The formula uses the absolute value of the gap between the two numbers, which strips away any sign, so the result is always zero or positive. A difference of zero means the values are identical. This is a deliberate consequence of the method being symmetric: since neither value is treated as the baseline, there is no direction for the figure to point, and therefore no negative outcome.

faqs.question: How do I find the percentage difference between two numbers?
faqs.answer: Subtract the smaller value from the larger to get the absolute gap, add the two numbers and halve them to get the average, then divide the gap by the average and multiply by 100. For 40 and 60, the gap is 20 and the average is 50, so 20 divided by 50 times 100 is a 40% difference. The order you enter the two numbers never affects the outcome.

title: Average Calculator
introEs: Find the mean, median, min and max of a list.
explanationEs: An average, or arithmetic mean, condenses a whole list of numbers into a single representative value: add every entry together and divide by how many there are. It answers what each item would be if the total were shared out equally, which is why it is the most common summary of a data set. The average calculator computes this along with the companion statistics that give it context: the median, sum, count, minimum and maximum. For the list 12, 18, 24 and 30, the sum is 84 across four values, so the mean is 84 divided by 4, which is 21. The mean is used because it accounts for every value and pairs naturally with totals, but it can be pulled off-centre by extreme entries, so an average calculator reports the median alongside it. The median is the middle value once the numbers are sorted, also 21 for this list, and it resists the distortion that a single outlier would cause. Students average grades, teachers average class scores, and analysts, scientists and finance teams average prices, times and measurements. Whenever a spread of numbers needs one dependable central figure, this average calculator delivers the mean and the supporting statistics together.
exampleEs: Sum = 84, count = 4, so mean = 84 ÷ 4 = 21. Median = (18 + 24) ÷ 2 = 21.

faqs.question: What is the difference between mean and median?
faqs.answer: The mean is the sum of all values divided by how many there are, so every number influences it. The median is the middle value once the list is sorted, so only the central position matters. When data is evenly spread the two agree, since both are 21 for 12, 18, 24 and 30, but when a few extreme values are present, the median stays closer to the typical entry.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the average of a list of numbers?
faqs.answer: Add all the numbers to get their sum, count how many there are, then divide the sum by the count. For 12, 18, 24 and 30 the sum is 84 and the count is 4, so the average is 84 divided by 4, which equals 21. The calculator does this instantly and also sorts the values to report the median, minimum and maximum at the same time.

faqs.question: When should I use the median instead of the mean?
faqs.answer: Use the median when your data contains outliers or is heavily skewed, such as incomes, house prices or response times, where a few very large values would drag the mean upward and misrepresent the typical case. The median ignores how far the extremes lie and reports only the middle value, so it often describes a normal entry more faithfully than the mean does for lopsided data.

faqs.question: How many numbers can I enter?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed limit; enter as many values as you need, separated by commas, spaces or new lines. The calculator reads them all, adds them for the sum, divides by the count for the mean, and sorts them to find the median, minimum and maximum. Mixing separators is fine, so pasting a column of figures or a comma-separated row both work without any reformatting.

faqs.question: Does the order of the numbers matter?
faqs.answer: No. The sum and the mean do not depend on order, and the calculator sorts the list internally before finding the median, minimum and maximum, so any arrangement gives the same results. Whether you enter 12, 18, 24, 30 or the same values shuffled, the mean stays 21 and the median stays 21. You can paste numbers in whatever order they happen to appear.

title: Square Root Calculator
introEs: Find the square root of any number.
explanationEs: The square root of a number is the value that, multiplied by itself, reproduces that number, so the square root of 144 is 12, because 12 times 12 is 144. It reverses squaring, unwinding an area back to the length of one side, which is exactly how the operation arises in geometry, physics and statistics. The square root calculator finds this value for any number from zero upward and returns it to several decimal places for precision. Every positive number has two roots that square to it, one positive and one negative, but the calculator reports the principal root, the non-negative one, because that is the value meant in almost all practical contexts. Zero has a single root of zero, and negative numbers have no real square root at all, since no real value squared is negative, which is why a square root calculator restricts its input to zero or greater. Roots appear constantly beyond the classroom: they scale distances through the Pythagorean theorem, define standard deviation in statistics, and set the sizing of squares and circles in design and engineering. Whenever squaring needs to be undone, this square root calculator returns the exact underlying value.

faqs.question: What is a square root?
faqs.answer: A square root of a number is a value that gives that number when multiplied by itself. Since 12 times 12 is 144, twelve is a square root of 144. The operation undoes squaring, so it turns an area back into the length of the side that produced it. This inverse relationship is why roots appear anywhere a squared quantity, such as a distance, a variance or an area, needs to be reversed.

faqs.question: Can I take the square root of a negative number?
faqs.answer: Not within the real numbers. No real value multiplied by itself gives a negative result, because a positive times a positive and a negative times a negative are both positive. The square root of a negative number is therefore called imaginary and lies outside ordinary arithmetic, which is why this calculator accepts only inputs of zero or greater and leaves negative entries without a real answer.

faqs.question: What is a principal square root?
faqs.answer: The principal square root is the non-negative one. Every positive number technically has two roots, one positive and one negative, that both square to it, since 12 and minus 12 each give 144. To keep results unambiguous, the calculator returns only the principal, positive value, which is the root intended in nearly every practical calculation involving lengths, distances and measured quantities.

faqs.question: Is a square root always a whole number?
faqs.answer: No. Only perfect squares like 144 have whole-number roots; most numbers have irrational roots that run on forever without repeating. The square root of 2, for example, is about 1.414214 and can never be written exactly as a fraction or a terminating decimal. The calculator handles both cases, returning an exact integer where one exists and a rounded decimal otherwise.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a square root by hand?
faqs.answer: For perfect squares, ask which number multiplied by itself gives your value: twelve works for 144 because 12 times 12 is 144. For other numbers, estimate between the two nearest perfect squares and refine, so a value between 121 and 144 has a root between 11 and 12. This guess-and-check narrowing is tedious, which is why a calculator is faster and far more precise for non-perfect squares.

title: Fraction Calculator
introEs: Add, subtract, multiply or divide two fractions.
explanationEs: A fraction represents a part of a whole as one number divided by another, a numerator over a denominator, and combining two fractions means finding the single fraction equal to their sum, difference, product or quotient. The challenge is that fractions can only be added or subtracted once they share a denominator, while multiplication and division follow different rules again. The fraction calculator handles all four operations and then reduces the outcome, so the answer arrives in its simplest form rather than an awkward, oversized ratio. To add or subtract, the tool rewrites both fractions over a common denominator, most simply the product of the two denominators, then works on the numerators; adding 1/2 and 1/3 becomes the numerator 1 times 3 plus 1 times 2 over 2 times 3, which is 5/6. To divide, it multiplies by the reciprocal of the second fraction. Every result is then divided top and bottom by the greatest common divisor, because a fraction calculator should present a value like 5/6 in lowest terms and its decimal, roughly 0.833333, alongside it. Students learning arithmetic, cooks scaling recipes, carpenters working in inches and anyone splitting quantities rely on this fraction calculator to combine fractions accurately without slips in the cross-multiplication.

faqs.question: How do I add fractions with different denominators?
faqs.answer: Give them a common denominator first. The simplest shared denominator is the product of the two, so for 1/2 and 1/3 you use sixths: 1/2 becomes 3/6 and 1/3 becomes 2/6. Add the numerators to get 5/6, then reduce if the result shares a common factor. Multiplication and division do not need a common denominator, but addition and subtraction always do.

faqs.question: Does the calculator simplify the answer?
faqs.answer: Yes, every result is reduced to lowest terms. After performing your chosen operation, the tool finds the greatest common divisor of the numerator and denominator and divides both by it, so nothing is left with a shared factor. That is why 1/2 plus 1/3 is reported as 5/6 rather than an unreduced equivalent. The decimal form, about 0.833333, is shown too for quick reference.

faqs.question: How do I divide by a fraction?
faqs.answer: Multiply by its reciprocal, flipping the second fraction upside down and multiplying. Dividing by 1/3 is the same as multiplying by 3/1, because division asks how many of the divisor fit into the dividend. The calculator applies this automatically when you choose the divide operation, then simplifies the product, so you never have to invert the fraction or reduce the result yourself.

faqs.question: How do I multiply fractions?
faqs.answer: Multiply the numerators together and the denominators together, with no common denominator needed. For 1/2 times 1/3 the numerators give 1 and the denominators give 6, so the product is 1/6. Multiplication is the most direct fraction operation because it works straight across. The calculator then reduces the result to lowest terms, cancelling any factor the top and bottom share.

faqs.question: What is a fraction as a decimal?
faqs.answer: It is the value you get by dividing the numerator by the denominator. Splitting 5 by 6 gives about 0.833333, which is why the calculator shows that alongside the fraction 5/6. Some fractions produce terminating decimals, like 1/2 equalling 0.5, while others repeat forever. The decimal form is handy for comparing fractions or plugging a result into further calculations that expect a plain number.

title: Ratio Calculator
introEs: Simplify a ratio and scale it proportionally.
explanationEs: A ratio compares two quantities by showing how many units of one correspond to units of the other, written with a colon as A to B. Two jobs come up constantly with ratios: reducing them to their simplest whole-number form and scaling them up while holding the proportion fixed. The ratio calculator does both, and also expresses the relationship as a single decimal for quick comparison. Simplifying divides both terms by their greatest common divisor, which leaves 16 : 9 unchanged but collapses 1920 : 1080 to the same 16 : 9. Scaling answers the practical question of what B must be if A becomes a given value. The tool keeps A to B constant, so setting A to 1920 against an original 16 : 9 returns B equal to 1920 times 9 divided by 16, which is 1080. Because the proportion never shifts, a ratio calculator lets you resize recipes, mixes, screen dimensions or map distances without recomputing the relationship from scratch. Designers matching aspect ratios, cooks and chemists holding a mixture's proportions, and model builders scaling plans all lean on this ratio calculator to simplify and rescale two-part relationships reliably.
exampleEs: 16 : 9 is already simplified. Scaling A to 1920 gives B = 1920 × 9 ÷ 16 = 1080.

faqs.question: How do I simplify a ratio?
faqs.answer: Divide both numbers by their greatest common divisor, the largest value that goes into each with no remainder. For 1920 : 1080 that divisor is 120, and dividing both terms by it leaves 16 : 9. The ratio still describes the same relationship, only with smaller numbers. If the two terms already share no common factor, the ratio is fully simplified as it stands.

faqs.question: What is a ratio as a decimal?
faqs.answer: It is the first term divided by the second, which turns the comparison into one plain number. A 16 : 9 ratio equals 16 divided by 9, about 1.78, meaning the first quantity is roughly 1.78 times the second. Decimals make ratios easy to rank and compare at a glance, and they slot directly into further calculations that expect a single value rather than a two-part expression.

faqs.question: How does scaling a ratio work?
faqs.answer: Scaling holds the proportion fixed while you change one term. Set a new value for A, and the calculator finds the B that keeps A to B equal to the original ratio. With a 16 : 9 ratio and A set to 1920, it returns 1080, because 1920 times 9 divided by 16 is 1080. This is how a single aspect ratio expands to any resolution without distorting the shape.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a ratio and a fraction?
faqs.answer: A fraction expresses a part of a single whole, while a ratio compares two separate quantities that may or may not belong to the same whole. A 16 : 9 ratio can be written as the fraction 16/9, and the arithmetic of simplifying is the same, but ratios often describe relationships like width to height or one ingredient to another, where thinking of a single whole would be misleading.

faqs.question: Can I use a ratio to find a missing value?
faqs.answer: Yes, that is exactly what the scaling field does. Given a known ratio and one new term, the calculator solves for the other so the proportion stays intact. Enter A as 1920 with an original 16 : 9 ratio and it returns B as 1080. The same cross-multiplication finds a missing first term if you know the second, which is how proportion problems in recipes and maps are solved.

title: GCF Calculator
introEs: Find the greatest common factor of numbers.
explanationEs: The greatest common factor of a set of numbers is the largest whole number that divides every one of them exactly, leaving no remainder. It captures the biggest chunk the numbers share, which is why it underpins reducing fractions, factoring expressions and splitting quantities into equal groups. The gcf calculator finds it for any list of whole numbers and, because the two ideas travel together, also returns the least common multiple. For 24, 36 and 60, the largest factor common to all three is 12, so the GCF is 12 while the LCM is 360. Rather than listing every factor of each number and hunting for the biggest match, the tool uses the Euclidean algorithm, which repeatedly replaces the larger number with the remainder of dividing it by the smaller until one becomes zero. That last non-zero value is the GCF, and the method stays fast even for large numbers, which is why a gcf calculator built on it handles long lists instantly by folding the result across the numbers pairwise. Students simplifying fractions, teachers setting factoring problems, and anyone dividing items into even portions turn to this gcf calculator for the largest shared divisor without trial and error.
exampleEs: The factors shared by 24, 36 and 60 peak at 12, so the GCF is 12 (and the LCM is 360).

faqs.question: What is the greatest common factor used for?
faqs.answer: Its most common job is simplifying fractions: dividing the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor reduces the fraction to lowest terms in one step. It also helps factor algebraic expressions, split items into the largest possible equal groups, and find common measurements. Anywhere you need the biggest amount two or more quantities share, the GCF is the number that answers it directly.

faqs.question: Is GCF the same as HCF and GCD?
faqs.answer: Yes, all three name the same value. Greatest Common Factor (GCF), Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) are interchangeable terms for the largest whole number that divides a set of numbers evenly. Textbooks in different countries favour different labels, but the calculation is identical, so a result of 12 for 24, 36 and 60 is correct whichever term your course uses.

faqs.question: How do I find the GCF of more than two numbers?
faqs.answer: Find the GCF of the first two, then take the GCF of that result with the next number, and continue through the list. Because a factor common to all must be common to each pair, this pairwise approach gives the right answer. For 24, 36 and 60 the shared factor works out to 12. The calculator performs these steps automatically for any list you enter.

faqs.question: What is the difference between GCF and LCM?
faqs.answer: The GCF is the largest number that divides all your values, while the least common multiple is the smallest number all your values divide into. One looks downward at shared factors, the other upward at shared multiples. For 24, 36 and 60 the GCF is 12 and the LCM is 360. They are linked: for two numbers, their product equals the GCF times the LCM.

faqs.question: Can I enter more than two numbers?
faqs.answer: Yes. Enter any list of whole numbers separated by commas, and the calculator finds the factor common to all of them at once. There is no practical limit on how many you include. It works through the list pairwise, so adding more numbers can only keep the GCF the same or lower it, never raise it, since the more values that must share a factor, the smaller that factor tends to be.

title: LCM Calculator
introEs: Find the least common multiple of numbers.
explanationEs: The least common multiple of a set of numbers is the smallest value that each of them divides into without a remainder, the first point at which their separate multiples all line up. It is the natural counterpart to the greatest common factor, and it is what you need whenever quantities repeating at different intervals have to synchronise. The lcm calculator returns it for any list of whole numbers and shows the greatest common factor beside it. For 4, 6 and 8, the smallest number every value divides into is 24, so the LCM is 24 while the GCF is 2. Rather than listing multiples of each number until a common one appears, the tool computes the LCM from the greatest common divisor: for two numbers it multiplies them and divides by their GCD, then applies the same step pairwise across the whole list. That shortcut is exact and fast, so an lcm calculator can handle large numbers that would be impractical to list out by hand. The most common use is adding or comparing fractions, where the LCM of the denominators gives the smallest common denominator; scheduling repeating events and aligning gear or cycle counts are others. Students, engineers and planners rely on this lcm calculator for the smallest shared multiple.
exampleEs: The smallest number divisible by 4, 6 and 8 is 24, so the LCM is 24 (their GCF is 2).

faqs.question: When do I need the least common multiple?
faqs.answer: Most often when adding or comparing fractions with unlike denominators: the LCM of the denominators is the smallest common denominator, which keeps the numbers as small as possible. It also solves timing problems, since when two events repeat at different intervals the LCM tells you when they next coincide. Aligning gear teeth, packaging counts and recurring schedules are other everyday uses for the least common multiple.

faqs.question: What is the difference between LCM and GCF?
faqs.answer: The least common multiple is the smallest number that all your values divide into, while the greatest common factor is the largest number that divides all of them. LCM looks upward to shared multiples; GCF looks downward to shared factors. For 4, 6 and 8 the LCM is 24 and the GCF is 2. The two are connected, since for any pair of numbers their product equals their LCM times their GCF.

faqs.question: How do I find the LCM of three or more numbers?
faqs.answer: Take the LCM of the first two numbers, then find the LCM of that result with the next number, and repeat through the list. Working pairwise like this reaches the smallest multiple shared by them all. For 4, 6 and 8 the process gives 24. The calculator does every step for you, so you can enter a long list of whole numbers and read the answer at once.

faqs.question: Can the LCM be one of the numbers?
faqs.answer: Yes. When one number is a multiple of all the others, that number is itself the least common multiple. For 4 and 8, since 8 is already divisible by 4, the LCM is 8 rather than something larger. In general the LCM is at least as big as the largest number in the set and never smaller, because it has to be divisible by every value present.

faqs.question: How is the LCM used to add fractions?
faqs.answer: Find the LCM of the denominators and rewrite each fraction over that common denominator, then add the numerators. Using the least common multiple rather than just multiplying the denominators keeps the numbers smaller and often avoids simplifying later. For denominators of 4, 6 and 8, the LCM is 24, so each fraction is converted to twenty-fourths before the numerators are combined.

title: Scientific Calculator
introEs: Apply scientific functions to any number.
explanationEs: A scientific calculator extends basic arithmetic with the functions that appear throughout algebra, trigonometry, statistics and the sciences: roots and powers, sines and cosines and their inverses, natural and base-ten logarithms, exponentials, factorials, reciprocals and absolute values. Rather than crowding every operation onto one screen, this scientific calculator applies a single chosen function to your input, which keeps each result unambiguous and easy to check. Trigonometric functions read the angle in whichever unit you select, degrees or radians, so sin of 45 degrees returns approximately 0.707107 when degrees are chosen. Several of these functions are only defined over part of the number line, and getting that wrong produces nonsense. Logarithms need a positive argument, arcsine and arccosine accept only values from minus 1 to 1, and factorials are defined for non-negative whole numbers. When an input falls outside a function's domain, the tool should return no result rather than a misleading one, which is exactly what it does by showing a dash instead. Students and teachers working through trigonometry and precalculus, engineers and physicists evaluating formulas, and analysts handling logarithmic or exponential data all depend on a scientific calculator for accurate function values that mental math and a basic four-function device cannot provide.

faqs.question: Does the calculator use degrees or radians?
faqs.answer: Both, and you choose the angle unit for trigonometric functions. Selecting degrees interprets an entry of 45 as 45 degrees, so sin of 45 degrees returns about 0.707107; selecting radians treats the same number as radians instead and gives a different result. Non-trigonometric functions such as logarithms, roots and factorials ignore the angle unit entirely, since they operate on plain numbers rather than angles.

faqs.question: Why do some inputs return no result?
faqs.answer: Certain functions are undefined for certain inputs, and the calculator shows a dash rather than invent a value. Logarithms require a positive argument, so the log of zero or a negative number has no real answer. Arcsine and arccosine accept only values between minus 1 and 1, and factorials need a non-negative whole number. When your entry falls outside the valid range, the blank result is the mathematically correct response.

faqs.question: What is the difference between ln and log?
faqs.answer: Both are logarithms but use different bases. Natural log, written ln, uses the base e, roughly 2.71828, and appears throughout calculus and growth models. The log button here uses base 10, which counts powers of ten and suits scientific notation and decibels. They answer the same kind of question, namely what exponent produces this number, but against different bases, so their outputs for the same input differ.

faqs.question: How large a factorial can it calculate?
faqs.answer: Factorials grow extremely fast, and above 170 the result exceeds the largest value standard floating-point numbers can hold. Beyond that point the calculator reports infinity rather than a finite figure, because the true answer is larger than the format can represent. For inputs up to 170, it returns the exact factorial, and it declines negative or fractional inputs since the ordinary factorial is defined only for non-negative whole numbers.

faqs.question: Can I use it for trigonometry homework?
faqs.answer: Yes. It evaluates sine, cosine and tangent along with their inverses arcsine, arccosine and arctangent, in either degrees or radians to match your assignment. Choosing degrees, sin of 45 degrees gives about 0.707107, the value you would expect on a standard unit circle. Set the angle unit before you compute, since the same number produces a different result in radians, and the inverse functions return the angle in your chosen unit.

title: Standard Deviation Calculator
introEs: Calculate the standard deviation, variance, and mean of a data set.
explanationEs:
Standard deviation is one of the most fundamental statistics, measuring how much individual values in a dataset deviate from the average. A low standard deviation indicates values cluster close to the mean; a high standard deviation signals wide spread.

The choice between population and sample standard deviation depends on your data. If you have data for every member of a group (e.g., all students in a class), use population standard deviation. If your data is a sample drawn from a larger group (e.g., 50 students surveyed from all students in a country), use sample standard deviation. The sample formula uses n−1 in the denominator (Bessel's correction) to produce an unbiased estimate of the true population standard deviation.

In practice, standard deviation is used everywhere: quality control (is a manufacturing process consistent?), finance (how volatile is a stock?), education (how spread are test scores?), and science (how precise are measurements?). Combined with the mean, standard deviation defines the normal distribution — roughly 68% of data falls within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three (the 68-95-99.7 rule).
exampleEs: For the dataset {2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9}, the mean is 5. Subtracting the mean and squaring each value, then averaging those squares gives a variance of 4. The square root of 4 is 2, so the population standard deviation is 2.

faqs.question: What is the difference between population and sample standard deviation?
faqs.answer: Population standard deviation (σ) is used when your dataset contains every member of the group you're studying. It divides the sum of squared deviations by N. Sample standard deviation (s) is used when your dataset is a subset of a larger population. It divides by n−1 (Bessel's correction) to avoid underestimating the true population standard deviation. In most real-world research scenarios, you're working with a sample, so use n−1.

faqs.question: What does a standard deviation of 0 mean?
faqs.answer: A standard deviation of exactly zero means every value in your dataset is identical — there is no variation whatsoever. For example, the dataset {5, 5, 5, 5} has a standard deviation of 0. In practice, a very low standard deviation (close to zero) indicates very little variability in your data, which could mean a highly consistent manufacturing process, very similar test scores, or stable measurements.

faqs.question: How do I interpret standard deviation in real life?
faqs.answer: Standard deviation tells you the 'typical' distance of data points from the average. For example, if test scores average 75 with a standard deviation of 10, most students scored between 65 and 85. In finance, a stock with high standard deviation is more volatile. In manufacturing, low standard deviation means consistent product quality. The 68-95-99.7 rule states that for normally distributed data, about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean.

faqs.question: Why is standard deviation preferred over variance?
faqs.answer: Standard deviation is preferred because it's expressed in the same units as the original data, making it intuitively interpretable. Variance is expressed in squared units, which can be difficult to relate to the original measurements. For example, if you measure heights in centimeters, the variance would be in cm², but standard deviation remains in cm. Standard deviation is also more directly used in statistical tests, confidence intervals, and the normal distribution.

faqs.question: Can standard deviation be negative?
faqs.answer: No, standard deviation can never be negative. It's calculated as the square root of variance, and variance is a sum of squared values (which are always non-negative) divided by a positive number. The minimum possible standard deviation is 0, which occurs only when all values in the dataset are identical. If you ever get a negative result, there's an error in the calculation — always double-check your inputs.

title: Mean, Median & Mode Calculator
introEs: Find the mean, median, mode, range, and sum of any data set instantly.
explanationEs:
Mean, median, and mode are the three measures of central tendency, and each summarizes a dataset with a single representative value in a different way. Knowing when to reach for each one is the core skill behind honest data analysis, which is why a mean median mode reading is usually reported as a group rather than in isolation.

The mean (arithmetic average) adds all values and divides by the count. It's the most commonly used measure but is sensitive to outliers. A few very high or very low values can pull the mean away from where most data falls.

The median is the middle value when data is sorted. It's robust to outliers and better represents 'typical' values in skewed distributions. For example, median income is often reported instead of mean income because a few billionaires can make the mean much higher than what most people earn.

The mode is the most frequently occurring value — the only measure that works for categorical (non-numerical) data. A dataset can have no mode, one mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal), or many modes (multimodal).

Together with range — the spread from the minimum to the maximum — these statistics give a quick yet powerful summary of any distribution's shape and center. Analysts, teachers, economists, and researchers lean on mean median mode figures to spot skew, compare groups, and choose the single number that best describes their data before running deeper tests.
exampleEs: For {2, 3, 4, 7, 7, 9}: mean = 32/6 ≈ 5.33; median = (4+7)/2 = 5.5 (average of 3rd and 4th values); mode = 7 (appears twice); range = 9−2 = 7.

faqs.question: When should I use mean vs median vs mode?
faqs.answer: Use mean when data is symmetrically distributed without significant outliers — it uses all data points and is most precise. Use median when data is skewed or has outliers (like income, home prices, or ages) — it better represents the 'typical' value. Use mode for categorical data (like most popular product color) or when you want the most common value in a dataset. In many analyses, reporting all three gives the most complete picture.

faqs.question: What if my data set has no mode or multiple modes?
faqs.answer: A dataset has no mode if every value appears exactly once — no value is more frequent than any other. A dataset has two modes (bimodal) if two values tie for the most frequent occurrence, and multimodal if more than two values tie. Our calculator reports all modes. Having no mode simply means there's no single most common value — this is actually common in continuous numerical data where repetition is unlikely.

faqs.question: How does adding an outlier affect mean vs median?
faqs.answer: Adding an extreme outlier can dramatically shift the mean but barely affects the median. For example, in {2, 3, 4, 5, 6} the mean is 4. Adding 1000 makes it {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1000} with a mean of 170 — far from where most data sits. But the median only shifts from 4 to (4+5)/2 = 4.5. This resilience makes median the preferred measure when outliers are expected, such as in income or housing price distributions.

faqs.question: What is the relationship between mean, median, and skewness?
faqs.answer: The relationship between mean and median reveals the shape of a distribution. If mean > median, the distribution is right-skewed (positively skewed) with a long tail toward higher values — common in income data. If mean < median, it's left-skewed (negatively skewed) with a long tail toward lower values. If mean ≈ median, the distribution is roughly symmetric. In a perfectly symmetric bell curve (normal distribution), mean, median, and mode are all equal.

faqs.question: Can the mean, median, and mode all be different numbers?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is common in real data. For example, in the set {1, 1, 2, 3, 10}: mode = 1 (appears twice), median = 2 (middle value), and mean = 17/5 = 3.4. The large outlier (10) pulls the mean up significantly, while the repeated small value (1) anchors the mode at the lower end. This is why statisticians report multiple measures of central tendency — each tells a different story about the data's distribution.

title: Z-Score Calculator
introEs: Calculate the z-score (standard score) to see how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.
explanationEs:
The z-score, also called the standard score, is a fundamental tool in statistics for comparing values from different distributions or understanding where a value falls relative to a group.

A z-score tells you exactly how many standard deviations above or below the mean a particular value is. A z-score of +2 means the value is 2 standard deviations above the mean; a z-score of −1.5 means it's 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

Z-scores enable comparison across different scales. For example, if a student scored 85 on a math test (mean 70, SD 10) and 72 on an English test (mean 65, SD 5), their math z-score is +1.5 and English z-score is +1.4 — so they performed slightly better in math relative to their peers, even though the raw scores differ.

Using the standard normal distribution table (Z-table), z-scores also map to percentile ranks. A z-score of +1.96 corresponds roughly to the 97.5th percentile. In many fields — medicine, education, finance — z-scores are used to identify outliers, normalize data, and build statistical tests. Because the calculation strips away the original units, a z-score places any measurement on one common scale, which is exactly what makes standardized comparison across different tests and datasets possible.
exampleEs: A test score of 85 with a class mean of 70 and standard deviation of 10 gives z = (85 − 70) / 10 = 1.5. This means the score is 1.5 standard deviations above average, placing it roughly at the 93rd percentile.

faqs.question: What is a good or bad z-score?
faqs.answer: There's no universally 'good' or 'bad' z-score — it depends entirely on context. In education, a high positive z-score means scoring above average, which is typically desirable. In quality control, z-scores far from 0 (either positive or negative) might indicate defects. In medical testing, z-scores far from 0 often flag abnormal results. Generally, z-scores between −2 and +2 include about 95% of values in a normal distribution, so anything beyond ±2 is considered unusual.

faqs.question: How do I convert a z-score to a percentile?
faqs.answer: Z-scores map to percentiles through the standard normal distribution. A z-score of 0 is at the 50th percentile (exactly average). A z-score of +1 is approximately the 84th percentile. A z-score of +2 is about the 97.7th percentile. A z-score of −1 is approximately the 16th percentile. For precise conversions, you'd use a standard normal distribution table (Z-table) or a statistical calculator. The general pattern: higher z-score = higher percentile rank.

faqs.question: What does a negative z-score mean?
faqs.answer: A negative z-score means the value is below the mean. For example, a z-score of −1.5 means the value is 1.5 standard deviations below average. Whether this is concerning depends on context: a body temperature z-score of −2 might indicate hypothermia, while a z-score of −0.5 on a test just means slightly below average. The magnitude (absolute value) tells you how far from average; the sign tells you the direction (above or below).

faqs.question: Can z-scores be used with any data distribution?
faqs.answer: Z-scores can be calculated for any numerical data, but their percentile interpretations only apply precisely when the data follows a normal (bell curve) distribution. For heavily skewed distributions or those with multiple peaks, a z-score of +2 may not correspond to the 97.7th percentile. In those cases, z-scores still measure distance from the mean in standard deviation units, which is useful for comparison and outlier detection — but interpret percentile mappings with caution.

faqs.question: How are z-scores used in real-world applications?
faqs.answer: Z-scores are used across many fields. In medicine, bone density z-scores compare a patient's density to age-matched peers, with z-scores below −2 indicating clinical concern. In finance, z-scores (Altman Z-score) help predict corporate bankruptcy risk. In education, standardized tests are often reported as z-scores or derived scores. In manufacturing, z-scores measure process capability (how many standard deviations between the mean and specification limits). In machine learning, z-score normalization (standardization) scales features to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

title: Combinations Calculator (nCr)
introEs: Calculate the number of ways to choose r items from a set of n items, where order doesn't matter.
explanationEs:
Combinations answer the question: 'In how many ways can I choose r items from a group of n, if the order I pick them doesn't matter?' This is written as C(n, r), nCr, or the binomial coefficient (n choose r).

The key distinction is between combinations and permutations. If you're choosing 3 people from a group of 10 for a committee (where it doesn't matter who is first, second, or third), use combinations: C(10, 3) = 120. But if you're assigning 3 people to the roles of President, VP, and Treasurer (where order matters), use permutations: P(10, 3) = 720.

Combinations appear everywhere in probability, statistics, and everyday life. Lottery odds are calculated using combinations (choosing 6 numbers from 49). In genetics, combinations count the number of possible gene combinations. In card games, combinations determine the number of possible hands.

The formula uses factorials (n! = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × ... × 1). For large values, the numbers grow extremely quickly — C(50, 25) is over 126 trillion, which is why lotteries are so hard to win. Because order is ignored, a combinations count always comes out smaller than the matching permutation count, and that gap widens sharply as r grows.
exampleEs: Choosing 3 players from a squad of 10 for a mini-game: C(10, 3) = 10! / (3! × 7!) = (10 × 9 × 8) / (3 × 2 × 1) = 720 / 6 = 120 ways.

faqs.question: What is the difference between combinations and permutations?
faqs.answer: The key difference is whether order matters. Combinations are used when the selection itself is what counts, regardless of the order items are arranged. Permutations are used when the order or arrangement of selected items matters. For example, choosing 3 flavors from 10 for a sampler plate is a combination (the plate is the same regardless of selection order). Arranging those 3 flavors in order from favorite to least favorite is a permutation. Permutations always equal or exceed combinations for the same n and r.

faqs.question: What does C(n, 0) and C(n, n) equal?
faqs.answer: C(n, 0) always equals 1 — there is exactly one way to choose nothing from any set. Similarly, C(n, n) always equals 1 — there is exactly one way to choose everything. These are important edge cases in combinatorics. C(n, 1) = n, because there are n ways to choose a single item from n items. These base cases are fundamental to Pascal's Triangle, where each number is the sum of the two numbers above it.

faqs.question: How do combinations relate to Pascal's Triangle?
faqs.answer: Pascal's Triangle is a direct representation of combinations. Each entry in the triangle at row n, position r equals C(n, r). For example, row 4 is: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 — which are C(4,0)=1, C(4,1)=4, C(4,2)=6, C(4,3)=4, C(4,4)=1. Pascal's Triangle reveals the symmetry of combinations: C(n, r) = C(n, n−r). This symmetry makes sense intuitively: choosing r items to include is equivalent to choosing n−r items to exclude.

faqs.question: What is the binomial coefficient and how does it relate to combinations?
faqs.answer: The binomial coefficient is just another name for C(n, r), written as (n choose r). It's called 'binomial' because it appears in the Binomial Theorem: (a + b)^n expands into a sum of terms, each with a binomial coefficient. For example, (a + b)^3 = C(3,0)a³ + C(3,1)a²b + C(3,2)ab² + C(3,3)b³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³. These coefficients (1, 3, 3, 1) match the third row of Pascal's Triangle.

faqs.question: How do I calculate combinations when n and r are very large?
faqs.answer: Standard factorial calculations become impractical for large values because the numbers grow astronomically fast (100! has 158 digits). Practical approaches include: canceling common factors before multiplying (C(100, 3) = (100 × 99 × 98) / (3 × 2 × 1) rather than computing 100! fully), using logarithms of factorials for computation, or using specialized big-integer libraries. Many statistical software packages handle large combinations precisely. For approximate values, Stirling's approximation can estimate factorials: n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)^n.

title: Probability Calculator
introEs: Calculate the probability of an event occurring given favorable and total outcomes.
explanationEs:
Probability quantifies the likelihood that a specific event will occur. It ranges from 0 (the event will never happen) to 1 (the event will definitely happen), and is often expressed as a percentage (0% to 100%).

The classical definition of probability — often called 'equally likely outcomes' — applies when every possible outcome has the same chance of occurring. For example, rolling a fair die has 6 equally likely outcomes. The probability of rolling a 4 is 1/6 ≈ 0.167 or 16.7%.

Probability underpins virtually every field: actuaries use it to set insurance premiums, doctors use it to interpret diagnostic test accuracy, gamblers use it to assess bets, weather forecasters express predictions as probabilities, and financial analysts use it to model market risk.

Beyond the basic formula, more complex probability calculations involve independent events (P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)), mutually exclusive events (P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)), and conditional probability (P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B)). The fundamental single-event case shown here is the starting point. Mastering these probability basics is the foundation for everything from insurance pricing to game strategy, and it is the first step before tackling compound or conditional problems.
exampleEs: Drawing a King from a standard 52-card deck: there are 4 Kings but we want any specific suit, say the King of Hearts: probability = 1/52 ≈ 0.0192 or 1.92%. Drawing any King: 4 favorable / 52 total = 0.0769 or 7.69%.

faqs.question: What is the difference between probability and odds?
faqs.answer: Probability and odds are related but different expressions of likelihood. Probability = favorable / total, ranging from 0 to 1. Odds = favorable / unfavorable (not total). For example, if you have 3 favorable outcomes out of 10 total, probability = 3/10 = 0.3, but odds = 3/7 ≈ 0.429 (or '3 to 7'). When odds are quoted 'for' an event, a higher number is better; when odds are quoted 'against,' a higher number means less likely. Sports betting uses odds; scientific and statistical work typically uses probability.

faqs.question: What does a probability of 0 or 1 mean?
faqs.answer: A probability of exactly 0 means the event is impossible — it cannot occur under any circumstances. For example, rolling a 7 on a standard 6-sided die has probability 0. A probability of exactly 1 means the event is certain — it will definitely occur. For example, rolling a number between 1 and 6 on a standard die has probability 1. In practice, few real-world events have probability exactly 0 or 1; most fall somewhere in between, expressing degrees of uncertainty.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the probability of multiple events?
faqs.answer: For independent events (one doesn't affect the other), use multiplication: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). For example, flipping two heads in a row: (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/4. For mutually exclusive events (both can't happen simultaneously), use addition: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). For non-exclusive events, use: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). The complement rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A) is useful for calculating 'at least one' probabilities.

faqs.question: What is conditional probability?
faqs.answer: Conditional probability is the probability of an event given that another event has already occurred, written P(A|B) = 'probability of A given B.' It's calculated as P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). For example, the probability of drawing a King given you already drew a red card: P(King|Red) = P(King and Red) / P(Red) = (2/52) / (26/52) = 2/26 ≈ 7.7%. Conditional probability is the foundation of Bayes' Theorem, which is used in medical diagnostics, spam filtering, and AI.

faqs.question: Why doesn't probability tell me what will actually happen?
faqs.answer: Probability describes long-run frequency and uncertainty, not individual outcomes. Even with a 99% probability, the remaining 1% can occur on any single trial. This is a fundamental feature, not a flaw — it reflects the inherent randomness in the universe. The Law of Large Numbers guarantees that as you repeat an experiment many times, the observed frequency approaches the theoretical probability. But in the short run, any outcome is possible regardless of its probability. This is why 'low probability' events still happen regularly in practice.

title: Factorial Calculator (n!)
introEs: Calculate the factorial of any non-negative integer. See results for large values too.
explanationEs:
The factorial function, denoted n!, multiplies a positive integer n by every positive integer smaller than itself down to 1. For example, 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

By mathematical convention, 0! = 1. This might seem counterintuitive, but it follows from the empty product rule (a product of no numbers equals the multiplicative identity, 1) and ensures that formulas for combinations and permutations work correctly for edge cases.

Factorials grow astonishingly fast — 10! is already 3,628,800, and 20! exceeds 2.4 quintillion. This explosive growth is directly responsible for how difficult it becomes to win lotteries or brute-force cryptographic keys. The number 52! (possible shuffles of a standard deck of cards) is approximately 8 × 10^67 — a number larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe, meaning every shuffle in history has almost certainly been unique.

Factorials appear everywhere in mathematics: in combinatorics (counting arrangements), in Taylor series expansions (sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − ...), in the Gamma function (which extends factorials to non-integers), and in statistics. This mix of a one-line definition and explosive growth is what makes the factorial one of the first big ideas students meet in combinatorics and one of the most useful tools for counting arrangements.
exampleEs: 8! = 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 40,320. This is also the number of ways to arrange 8 books on a shelf in a different order each time.

faqs.question: Why does 0! equal 1?
faqs.answer: Zero factorial equals 1 by definition, and there are several ways to understand why this makes sense. Mathematically, it follows the 'empty product' convention: a product containing no factors equals 1 (just as a sum of no terms equals 0). Practically, it ensures the combination formula C(n, 0) = 1 works correctly — there is exactly one way to choose nothing from a set. It also satisfies the recurrence relation n! = n × (n−1)!: plugging in n=1 gives 1! = 1 × 0!, so 0! must be 1.

faqs.question: What is the largest factorial a calculator can compute?
faqs.answer: This depends on the numerical precision of the calculator. Standard double-precision floating-point numbers (used in most computing, including JavaScript) can represent factorials up to 170! (≈7.26 × 10^306) before exceeding the maximum representable value and becoming 'Infinity.' For exact integer results of larger factorials, you need big-integer arithmetic. Python's built-in integers handle arbitrarily large factorials. 171! ≈ 1.24 × 10^309, which exceeds the IEEE 754 double-precision maximum of about 1.80 × 10^308.

faqs.question: How are factorials used in combinations and permutations?
faqs.answer: Factorials are the building blocks of counting arrangements. Permutations (ordered arrangements) of r items from n: P(n, r) = n! / (n−r)!. Combinations (unordered selections) of r items from n: C(n, r) = n! / (r! × (n−r)!). For example, arranging 3 books from a shelf of 5 in different orders: P(5,3) = 5!/2! = 60. Choosing any 3 books from 5 regardless of order: C(5,3) = 5!/(3!×2!) = 10. Factorials also appear in probability distributions like the Poisson distribution.

faqs.question: What is the Gamma function and how does it relate to factorial?
faqs.answer: The Gamma function Γ(n) is an extension of the factorial function to non-integer and complex numbers. For positive integers, Γ(n) = (n−1)!. So Γ(5) = 4! = 24. The Gamma function is defined through an integral formula that works for all positive real numbers and complex numbers with a positive real part. This allows us to compute 'factorials' of non-integers: for example, Γ(1.5) = 0.5! × 2 ≈ 0.886. The Gamma function appears throughout statistics, physics, and engineering.

faqs.question: Why do factorials grow so incredibly fast?
faqs.answer: Factorials grow super-exponentially because each additional factor is larger than the previous one. Exponential growth (like 2^n) multiplies by the same factor each time. Factorial growth multiplies by an ever-increasing factor. By Stirling's approximation, n! ≈ √(2πn) × (n/e)^n, which grows much faster than any exponential function. This rapid growth is why the number of possible arrangements of large sets is astronomically large — 52 playing cards can be shuffled into more unique arrangements than there are atoms in the observable universe.

title: Exponent Calculator
introEs: Calculate base raised to a power (bⁿ). Handles any real exponent including fractions and negatives.
explanationEs:
Exponentiation is a mathematical operation where a base number is multiplied by itself a specified number of times. It is the third core operation built on repetition — addition repeats counting, multiplication repeats addition, and an exponent repeats multiplication. The expression b^n (read 'b to the power of n' or 'b raised to the nth power') means: multiply b by itself n times.

Exponents follow important rules that make calculations easier: b^m × b^n = b^(m+n), (b^m)^n = b^(m×n), b^0 = 1 (for any non-zero b), b^(-n) = 1/b^n, and b^(1/n) = the nth root of b.

Fractional exponents are particularly powerful: 4^(0.5) = √4 = 2, 8^(1/3) = ∛8 = 2, 32^(0.2) = ⁵√32 = 2. This connects exponentiation to roots.

Exponents also tame very large and very small numbers through scientific notation, where a value is written as a number times a power of 10. Writing 300,000,000 as 3 × 10^8, or 0.0000004 as 4 × 10^(−7), keeps figures compact and readable across science and engineering.

Exponential growth appears everywhere in nature and technology: compound interest, population growth, radioactive decay, and Moore's Law (the doubling of transistors roughly every 18 months). A firm grasp of exponents is essential for science, engineering, finance, and computer science.
exampleEs: 2^10 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 1,024. This is why 1 kilobyte = 2^10 = 1,024 bytes in binary computing.

faqs.question: What is anything to the power of 0?
faqs.answer: Any non-zero number raised to the power of 0 equals 1. This follows from the exponent rule b^n / b^n = b^(n−n) = b^0, and any number divided by itself is 1. So b^0 = 1 for any b ≠ 0. The expression 0^0 is mathematically indeterminate (it leads to conflicting values depending on how you approach it), but in many combinatorial contexts, it's defined as 1 for convenience. This rule is essential for polynomials and the binomial theorem.

faqs.question: How do negative exponents work?
faqs.answer: A negative exponent means take the reciprocal of the positive exponent result: b^(-n) = 1/b^n. For example, 2^(-3) = 1/2^3 = 1/8 = 0.125. Negative exponents are not negative numbers — they represent fractions less than 1 (for bases greater than 1). This rule is fundamental in scientific notation: 10^(-3) = 0.001 (one thousandth). Negative exponents also appear in physics for units like m/s² = m × s^(-2).

faqs.question: What are fractional exponents?
faqs.answer: Fractional exponents represent roots. The rule is b^(1/n) = the nth root of b, and b^(m/n) = (nth root of b)^m = nth root of b^m. For example: 4^(1/2) = √4 = 2; 8^(1/3) = ∛8 = 2; 16^(3/4) = (fourth root of 16)^3 = 2^3 = 8. This connects the exponent operation to root extraction and explains why square roots, cube roots, etc. are just special cases of exponentiation with fractional powers.

faqs.question: What is the difference between exponential growth and linear growth?
faqs.answer: Linear growth adds the same amount each time (e.g., saving $100 per month: $100, $200, $300...). Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each time (e.g., 10% compound interest: $1,000, $1,100, $1,210, $1,331...). In the short term, linear and exponential growth may look similar. Over time, exponential growth becomes enormously larger — this is why compound interest is so powerful, and why viral diseases spread so rapidly. Mathematically, any exponential eventually outpaces any polynomial (including linear).

faqs.question: What happens when you raise a negative number to a fractional exponent?
faqs.answer: Raising a negative number to a fractional exponent with an even denominator produces a complex (imaginary) number in standard math, since you'd need to take an even root of a negative number. For example, (-4)^(1/2) = √(-4) = 2i (where i is the imaginary unit). For odd denominators, the result is real: (-8)^(1/3) = ∛(-8) = -2. Most calculators, including ours, return NaN (not a number) for cases that would yield complex results, since complex number support requires a different representation.

title: Logarithm Calculator
introEs: Calculate the logarithm of any number to any base, including natural log (ln) and log base 10.
explanationEs:
The logarithm is the inverse operation of exponentiation. If 10^3 = 1000, then log₁₀(1000) = 3. If 2^8 = 256, then log₂(256) = 8. Logarithms answer the question: 'What exponent do I need to raise base b to, in order to get x?'

Three logarithms are especially common. Log base 10 (common log, log₁₀ or just 'log') is used in pH scales, the Richter scale for earthquakes, and decibels for sound. Natural log (ln, log base e where e ≈ 2.718) appears throughout calculus, physics, and the mathematics of growth and decay — interest, population, radioactive decay all involve natural logs. Log base 2 (log₂) is fundamental to information theory and computer science — binary systems, data compression, and algorithm complexity (O(log n)) all use log₂.

The change-of-base formula (log_b(x) = ln(x)/ln(b)) allows any logarithm to be computed using the natural log or common log, which is how calculators and computers implement it.

Before electronic calculators, logarithms were the fastest way to multiply large numbers by hand: printed log tables and the slide rule turned multiplication into simple addition. That same inverse relationship with exponents is why the logarithm remains the natural tool for solving any equation where the unknown sits in the exponent, from carbon dating to compound-interest problems.
exampleEs: log₁₀(1000) = 3 because 10³ = 1,000. The common logarithm of 1,000 is 3. This is why the pH scale spans from 0 to 14 with each step representing a 10× difference in acidity.

faqs.question: What is the natural logarithm (ln) and why is it special?
faqs.answer: The natural logarithm uses the mathematical constant e (≈ 2.71828) as its base. What makes e special is that it's the unique number where the function e^x has a derivative equal to itself — it models continuous growth and decay perfectly. The natural log appears in compound interest (when compounded continuously), probability distributions (normal distribution, Poisson), entropy in information theory, and countless physics equations. While log base 10 is convenient for human calculation, ln is the 'natural' choice mathematically and scientifically.

faqs.question: Why does log of a negative number not exist (in real numbers)?
faqs.answer: No real number exponent can make a positive base produce a negative result. Since b^x is always positive for positive b (e.g., 10^x is always positive), there's no real x such that b^x = negative number. Therefore, the logarithm of a negative number is undefined in real numbers. In complex number mathematics, logarithms of negative numbers can be defined (using complex exponents), but for everyday calculations, log(x) requires x > 0. Attempting log(0) is also undefined — it would require an exponent of −∞.

faqs.question: How do logarithmic scales work in the real world?
faqs.answer: Logarithmic scales compress large ranges into manageable numbers. The Richter scale: each step is 10× more energy — a magnitude 7 earthquake is 10× stronger than magnitude 6, and 1,000× stronger than magnitude 4. Sound decibels: every 10 dB increase is 10× more sound intensity. pH: each unit represents a 10× change in hydrogen ion concentration; pH 4 is 100× more acidic than pH 6. These scales allow us to compare quantities spanning many orders of magnitude on a single, human-readable scale.

faqs.question: What are the key logarithm rules I should know?
faqs.answer: The four fundamental logarithm rules are: Product rule — log(a × b) = log(a) + log(b); Quotient rule — log(a/b) = log(a) − log(b); Power rule — log(a^n) = n × log(a); Change of base — log_b(x) = log_a(x) / log_a(b). These rules were historically important because they turned multiplication into addition (used in slide rules and log tables). Today, they're essential for solving exponential equations: if 2^x = 50, then x = log₂(50) = log(50)/log(2) ≈ 5.64.

faqs.question: What is log base 2 used for in computing?
faqs.answer: Log base 2 (log₂) is fundamental in computer science and information theory. Binary counting uses base 2, so log₂(n) tells you how many bits are needed to represent n states: log₂(256) = 8 bits (1 byte), log₂(65,536) = 16 bits. Algorithm complexity often grows as O(log n) — binary search, balanced binary trees, and divide-and-conquer algorithms all have log₂ complexity. In information theory, log₂ measures information in bits: the probability p of an event carries −log₂(p) bits of information.

title: Modulo Calculator
introEs: Calculate the remainder of a division operation (a mod b) with the quotient.
explanationEs:
The modulo operation (often written as %, mod, or a mod b) returns the remainder when dividing one number by another. For example, 17 mod 5 = 2, because 17 = 5 × 3 + 2 (five goes into 17 three times, with 2 left over).

Modulo is one of the most fundamental operations in programming and number theory. In code, it's typically the % operator. It's used constantly in everyday programming: determining if a number is even (n % 2 == 0), wrapping around arrays (index = i % length), clock arithmetic (hours = (current + elapsed) % 12), and color cycling in UIs.

In mathematics, modular arithmetic (working with remainders) is the foundation of cryptography. The RSA encryption algorithm, which secures most internet communications, is built entirely on modular exponentiation. The last digits of large exponential calculations, determined by mod, create the one-way functions that make encryption secure.

Modulo also appears in checksum algorithms (credit card number validation), hash functions, random number generators, and scheduling problems. Whenever a value must wrap within a fixed range — an hour on a clock, a day of the week, a pixel column, or a slot in a hash table — the modulo operation is usually the cleanest way to express that wrap-around in a single step.
exampleEs: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2. So 17 mod 5 = 2, and the quotient is 3. Verification: 5 × 3 + 2 = 15 + 2 = 17 ✓

faqs.question: What is modulo used for in programming?
faqs.answer: Modulo is one of the most frequently used operations in programming. Common uses include: checking if a number is even or odd (n % 2 == 0 means even); wrapping indices for circular data structures (array[i % length] cycles through an array indefinitely); clock arithmetic (hour = (current_hour + hours_to_add) % 12); generating repeating patterns; implementing hash tables (hash % table_size maps any hash to a valid index); and creating cycles in animations (frame % total_frames). It's also central to cryptographic algorithms.

faqs.question: How does modulo work with negative numbers?
faqs.answer: Modulo with negative numbers can give different results depending on the programming language or mathematical convention used. In most mathematical contexts, the result has the same sign as the divisor (b). In Python: −7 mod 3 = 2. In C/Java/JavaScript, % gives the remainder with the sign of the dividend: −7 % 3 = −1. Our calculator uses the mathematical floor-based definition. The two are equivalent for positive numbers; for negative numbers, adjust with: if (result < 0) result += b to get the positive modulo.

faqs.question: What is modular arithmetic?
faqs.answer: Modular arithmetic is a system of integer arithmetic where numbers 'wrap around' upon reaching a certain value (the modulus). On a 12-hour clock, after 12 comes 1 (not 13) — that's mod 12. Days of the week cycle mod 7. Modular arithmetic follows its own algebra: you can add, subtract, and multiply numbers modulo m, and the results stay within 0 to m−1. This system has deep applications in cryptography, computer science, calendaring algorithms, and abstract algebra (group theory and ring theory).

faqs.question: What is the difference between modulo and remainder?
faqs.answer: For positive numbers, modulo and remainder are the same. The distinction arises with negative numbers. The mathematical modulo operation (used in number theory) always returns a non-negative result in [0, b−1]. The programming remainder (%) typically returns a result with the same sign as the dividend. For example: −7 mod 3 = 2 (mathematical), but −7 % 3 = −1 (C-style remainder). Both are useful; the mathematical modulo is preferred in cryptography and number theory, while the C-style remainder is what most programming languages implement with %.

faqs.question: How is modulo used in cryptography?
faqs.answer: Modular arithmetic is the mathematical backbone of modern cryptography. RSA encryption uses modular exponentiation: given large primes p and q, their product n = pq creates a 'trapdoor' — it's easy to compute m^e mod n (encrypt), but computationally infeasible to reverse without knowing the private key. The Diffie-Hellman key exchange uses discrete logarithms in modular arithmetic. AES encryption uses operations in a finite field (arithmetic modulo an irreducible polynomial). Without modular arithmetic, public-key cryptography — and therefore secure web browsing, banking, and messaging — would not be possible.

title: Mortgage Calculator
introEs: Estimate your monthly mortgage payment.
explanationEs: Your monthly mortgage payment is the fixed amount you send your lender each month to repay a home loan, split between interest on the outstanding balance and principal that steadily reduces what you owe. Knowing this number before you shop matters because it decides whether a home fits your budget and how lenders judge affordability against your income. This mortgage calculator derives the loan amount by subtracting your down payment from the home price, then applies the standard fixed-rate amortization formula so every payment across the term is identical. That formula is used because it guarantees the balance reaches exactly zero at the final payment while front-loading interest — early payments are mostly interest, later ones mostly principal. A larger down payment or a shorter term lowers the total interest a mortgage calculator will project, sometimes dramatically. Homebuyers, real estate agents and loan officers rely on a mortgage calculator to compare offers, test how rate changes ripple through the monthly cost, and set a realistic price ceiling. Remember the result covers principal and interest only; property taxes, homeowners insurance, private mortgage insurance and HOA dues are billed separately and can add hundreds of dollars to your true monthly housing cost.
exampleEs: A $320,000 loan at 6.5% over 30 years (360 payments) gives a monthly principal-and-interest payment of about $2,022.

faqs.question: What is a good interest rate on a mortgage?
faqs.answer: A competitive rate depends on the market, your credit score, the loan term and your down payment. Borrowers with strong credit and 20% down typically secure the lowest advertised rates, while lower scores pay a premium. Even a quarter-point difference changes thousands over a 30-year loan. Compare offers from several lenders on the same day, since rates move daily, and always check the APR, which folds in fees.

faqs.question: How much should my down payment be?
faqs.answer: Twenty percent is the classic benchmark because it removes private mortgage insurance and shrinks the loan, but many buyers put down far less. Conventional loans can start near 3%, FHA loans at 3.5%, and some VA and USDA loans require nothing down. A bigger down payment lowers your monthly payment and total interest, yet draining your savings for it can leave you exposed, so balance both goals.

faqs.question: How accurate is this mortgage calculator?
faqs.answer: The math is exact for a fixed-rate loan: it reproduces an amortization schedule to the cent. It is only an estimate of your true housing cost because it excludes property taxes, homeowners and mortgage insurance, HOA fees and closing costs. Adjustable-rate mortgages also reset after their intro period, which this fixed-rate model does not capture. Treat the principal-and-interest figure as reliable and add the escrow items separately.

faqs.question: What is the difference between principal and interest?
faqs.answer: Principal is the portion of each payment that reduces the balance you actually borrowed; interest is the lender's charge for lending it, calculated on the remaining balance. Early in the loan the balance is large, so most of your payment is interest. As the balance falls, more of each fixed payment goes to principal. This is why paying extra toward principal early saves a disproportionate amount of interest.

faqs.question: Can I use this for a refinance?
faqs.answer: Yes. Enter your new loan amount as the home price with a zero down payment, plus the new rate and remaining term, and the tool projects the refinanced payment. Compare it against your current payment to see the monthly savings, then weigh that against closing costs to find your break-even point. A refinance that lowers the payment by extending the term can still raise total interest paid.

title: Compound Interest Calculator
introEs: See how savings grow with compound interest.
explanationEs: Compound interest is the growth you earn when interest is added back to your balance and then earns interest of its own, so the account grows faster the longer it runs. The future value shown here is the projected balance once that snowball effect has compounded your initial deposit and every monthly contribution to the end of the period.
